speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Last year, Parliament amended the Broadcasting Act through the Online Safety Bill, which targets harmful online content such as advocacy of suicide and self-harm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is growing international consensus that new rules and levers are needed to combat criminal harms online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is also growing recognition that proactive approaches are needed to prevent such harms, and that Government efforts alone will not be enough.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The United Kingdom (UK), the European Union (EU), Germany and Australia have or are introducing new laws in this regard.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They have been useful references as we formulated our proposals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In general, we have taken a targeted approach, focusing on areas that are most problematic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have also taken a pragmatic and collaborative approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, we recognise and encourage initiatives by online services to improve online safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But we also know that they tend to be designed for a global user base and do not cater to the unique circumstances in specific locations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where we have identified a need for additional measures to tackle risks of criminal activities, it will be better to require them by law than to leave things to chance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The specific interventions should however be designed for ease of implementation, with strong emphasis on effective outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, the Bill makes special provisions for scams and malicious cyber activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such activities tend to unfold with great speed and scale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They inflict great harms on the victims, not just in terms of financial losses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Members would be familiar with the use of Directions to restrict the exposure of users in Singapore to online criminal content and activity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Directions are also a feature of the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA), the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act (FICA) and the Broadcasting Act (BA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: What criminal offences can Directions be used for?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These are criminal offences that affect national security, national harmony, and individual safety, and which have an online nexus.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They are specified in the First Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 6(1)(a) provides the legal threshold for Directions to be issued against online activity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Directions can be issued only when there is reasonable suspicion that a specified offence under Part 1 of the First Schedule has been committed and the online activity is in furtherance of that offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Designated officers will issue Directions for criminal offences under their agency's purview.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, designated officers from the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) will be authorised to issue Directions for offences under the Misuse of Drugs Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While designated officers may be sited in several agencies, a competent authority sited under the Singapore Police Force (SPF) will serve as a single point of contact across the Government, for recipients of Directions, such as online service providers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 8 to 12 set out the scope of the five types of Direction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, where the Police have reasonable suspicion that an account on a social media service is being used for unlicensed moneylending activity, they can issue the social media service provider: one, a Disabling Direction, so that the offending post or page is prevented from reaching a person in Singapore; or two, an Account Restriction Direction, so that an offending account is prevented from interacting with persons in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As a second example, a Stop Communication Direction may be issued to someone who posts text or images, inciting violence against people of a certain race.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The use of Directions limits the reach of criminals and prevents more persons from being exposed to the harm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For scams and malicious cyber activities, we will however need a different approach, one which is more proactive and pre-emptive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Many scams and malicious cyber activities are carried out through deception.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, scammers may create online accounts or websites that seem authentic and legitimate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such accounts or websites are then used to convince victims to transit to another platform, where they are then targeted for scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Unfortunately, the initial contacting and grooming of victims may not yet constitute a criminal offence, even if they are a necessary step.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As a result, they may not cross the threshold of reasonable suspicion for Directions to be issued.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Malicious actors are also quite "kiasu", in the sense of preparing much more than the bare minimum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, thousands of blank websites are created in advance, with domain names that resemble those of legitimate organisations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: When the malicious actor is ready to strike, these blank websites are swiftly activated, populated with scam content and pushed out to the public, who may fall prey within minutes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But until these blank websites and preparatory locations are activated, they may also not cross the threshold of reasonable suspicion for Directions to be issued.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is when there is suspicion or reason to believe that any online activity is being carried out in preparation for or as part of the commission of a scam or malicious cyber activity offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition, we will require providers of designated online services to put in place systems and processes to counter possible offences under the Second Schedule.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For now, the only group specified within the Second Schedule will be scam and malicious cyber activity offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But this approach allows us to respond more quickly if new classes of offences emerge which also require counter actions by designated online services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Law enforcement agencies obtain information only when Police reports are filed by victims, or through online trawling, which is not exhaustive and is more akin to finding a needle in a haystack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On the other hand, online services have direct and full access to relevant data about activities on their platform, and can also perform analytics to detect and respond to crime on their platform.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Through successful partnerships with the Police, online service providers have also found that it helps them plug information gaps and take more effective actions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, a scammer may first approach a victim through an online service but carry out the scam on a different online service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The first online service may not be aware of the scam and will act to identify and remove the source only when alerted by the Police.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such collaboration will be promoted through codes of practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Their requirements will be framed in terms of outcomes which designated online services must meet.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This gives a provider the flexibility to customise its approach depending on the nature of its service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The competent authority will consult and work with the providers of designated online services in developing the codes of practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The codes will be updated periodically in response to new and evolving threats, and technological developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 24 provides that the competent authority may issue the provider of a designated online service an Implementation Directive to put in place any system, process, or measure, if it is satisfied that this is necessary or expedient to address a relevant offence under the Second Schedule.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Unlike codes of practice, an Implementation Directive will be specific and prescriptive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, the competent authority may issue an Implementation Directive for a designated online service to put in place a specific form of multi-factor authentication to protect against the misuse of accounts to commit crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We are providing for such Directives as a complement to the codes of practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, where there may be an urgent need to put in place a specific measure to address the proliferation of a specific scam operation, an Implementation Directive would be more effective in this instance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 20 provides for the competent authority to designate online services that would be subject to the codes of practice and Implementation Directives to be applied against offences in the Second Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In designating online services, we will consider the extent and impact of the harms relating to the specified offence groups, the reach of the online service, the design and nature of the online service and any other relevant factors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 28 to 31 provide the competent authority with powers to issue Access Blocking Orders, App Removal Orders or Service Restriction Orders, where there has been non-compliance with a Direction, a Rectification Notice, an Implementation Directive, or another Order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In other words, Orders are intended to be an escalatory enforcement measure taken only where necessary, if there has been non-compliance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Their purpose is to limit the further exposure of persons in Singapore to the criminal activity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Orders operate alongside and do not replace other possible measures that we can take for non-compliance, such as prosecution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For Directions and Orders, an appellant must first seek reconsideration from the agency that gave the Direction or Order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If the reconsideration request is unsuccessful, the appellant can then appeal to a specialised Reviewing Tribunal under clause 18 or 37.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This allows timely and efficient remedies to be delivered via an independent channel instead of via general appeal to the Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such appeals involve assessments of the online landscape and policy considerations on how regulatory levers should be applied.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, the Police may require account information relating to persons who are distributing child sex abuse material from an online service provider that is not based in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This Bill is calibrated to allow us to respond more effectively to online criminal harms while enabling us to continue to enjoy the many benefits which the Internet has brought us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will reiterate why the WP did not support previous Bills concerning online content.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is important to highlight to Singaporeans that each piece of legislation needs to be scrutinised on its own merits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government must be made to justify each statute it wishes to pass by this House, including those that restrict Singaporeans' access to online content.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will set out why we support the current Bill as a whole.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, despite my general agreement with the Bill, I will raise questions for the Minister on specific points of concern.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In its press release on 8 May, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) called this Bill, "the next piece in our suite of legislation, including the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA), Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act (FICA) and the recently amended Broadcasting Act to better protect the public in Singapore from various harms in the online space." The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) groups these four Acts together – the Broadcasting Act, POFMA, FICA and now, if I may coin the obvious acronym, OCHA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, we need to remind ourselves in this House and we need to remind Singaporeans generally that these statutes are very different from one another.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Three points connect these statutes: firstly, they relate to online content; secondly, the Government says that these laws are needed to protect Singaporeans from harm; thirdly, the Government can implement broad, powerful measures to restrict Singaporeans' access to online content and to impose severe penalties on individuals and entities for non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: OCHA targets online content that could result in Singaporeans being victims of scams and other crimes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: POFMA and FICA restrict the access of Singaporeans to information that the Government considers false, manipulative or constitutes foreign interference in our domestic affairs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Reasonable people can disagree with the Government on what types of online content are harmful and whether Singaporeans need to be protected from them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Reasonable people can also desire that the Government not be given draconian powers that could be used, whether now or by future governments, to stifle points of view different from those of the government of the day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP was also of the view that the wording in FICA such as "is likely to" and "where the Minister suspects" creates low thresholds of proof that could be unfairly used against individuals or entities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP proposed more than 40 amendments which we opined would allow FICA to achieve its aims of curbing unwanted foreign influence, while at the same time ensuring appropriate checks on the Government that protect the rights of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In certain cases, they would not be neutral parties, but would be making decisions as interested parties.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For instance, if a Government decision is criticised in an article published on a website, it is the Minister himself or herself who decides whether the article is true or false.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister would be able to make such a decision with limited oversight by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The High Court cannot inquire into the merits of a Minister's POFMA decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the powers under POFMA are extreme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If a Correction Order is made, an entire website is blocked, not just the offending article.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My view is that when websites are blocked under POFMA, it is Singaporeans who lose out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans are not able to read alternate viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If such alternate viewpoints are false, the Government can counter those viewpoints by publishing the facts as it sees them in the mainstream local media, both in print as well as online.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The recent case involving Asia Sentinel is instructive on how POFMA can be deployed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government recently issued a POFMA Correction Direction to Asia Sentinel, a California-registered publication, over an article titled, "Singapore kills a Chicken to Scare the Monkeys." Asia Sentinel took certain actions to comply, but the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) said, "While Asia Sentinel carried the Correction Notices, this was not done in compliance with the requirements of the Correction Direction for the respective Correction Notices to be situated at the top of the article and at the top of the main page of the website." I believe that Asia Sentinel placed the Correction Notice at the top of the article but did not place it at the top of the main page of the website.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The article and the website are no longer accessible by computers and smart phones with Singapore Internet Protocol (IP) addresses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In particular, I find it draconian to expect a news website to place a Correction Direction at the top of the main page of the website.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My concern is not for Asia Sentinel in itself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is of not much concern to me whether they lose readership or revenue by being blocked in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What I do care about is that I and other Singaporeans cannot access Asia Sentinel to read the article in question and decide what we think about it for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, that smacks of the Government wanting to punish the publishers of the website, rather than merely wanting to correct falsehoods in a specific article.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Government must have many tools at its disposal to ensure that its viewpoint is available to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is it really in the best interest of Singapore Citizens that the Government blocks not only an article the Government deems false, but an entire publication?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What if The New York Times or The Financial Times were to republish the Asia Sentinel article or any other POFMA-sanctioned article?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Singapore Government seriously mean to block either The New York Times or The Financial Times if it refuses to publish the Correction Notices in the required format?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would this blocking be in the best interest of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP agrees that it is necessary to protect Singaporeans from scams and other crimes that may be perpetrated using online methods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe it is right for the authorities to have available the use of Part 2 Directions against those who control relevant material or websites, online service providers, Internet service providers and app stores.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am sure that legitimate business operators in these areas would have no objection to cooperating with Singapore authorities to protect those who live here from online criminal harms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In particular, I support the development of codes of practice for designated online services as provided for in Part 4.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, a proactive approach rather than a reactive one is certainly important in view of how quickly online scams evolve.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Overall, the WP's assessment is that OCHA is very different from POFMA and FICA when it comes to the online harms targeted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This Bill deserves the support of the House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first question for the Minister is, what exactly is the difference between the use in Part 2, specifically clause 6(1), of the words "reasonably suspects" compared to the word "suspects" in limb A and limb B of the clause specifically?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MHA's press release acknowledges that the word "suspects" has a lower threshold than "reasonably suspects", but what is the practical effect of this difference in the context of combating online crimes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps the Minister could explain this distinction using the standards of proof used in our Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could the standards on a balance of probabilities, prima facie or reasonable doubt help us understand the difference better?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While in principle, a proactive approach in having codes of practice is good, the fact that there are sanctions for non-compliance reiterates the importance, if not the critical role, designated online services and other intermediary services play to disrupt scammers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under Part 4 of the Bill, the Government may issue Rectification Notices and Implementation Directives to designated online services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Non-compliance with notices or directives attract prosecution and severe fines that can go into the millions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister give details of how codes of practice will be developed, including what consultations and engagements will be undertaken with the industry?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, Mr Deputy Speaker, how would these codes of practice apply in practice to disrupt online scams?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the Minister gave a broad outline in her opening speech, but let me suggest a particular context for consideration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The days of receiving phone calls from people pretending to be Immigration, Ministry of Health (MOH) or bank officers are fast becoming yesterday's scams.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today's online scams that lure individuals – one that was recounted to me at this Monday's Meet-the-People Session just two days ago – are very sophisticated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A resident was lured by an offer of a supposedly genuine job to raise the profile of products sold on e-commerce platforms such as Qoo10.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The resident received a payment for services rendered on the first day of her assignment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Convinced that the arrangement was legitimate as money had been transferred to the resident, the resident got trapped in a quasi-investment scam, hoping to see more returns and thereby increased her engagement with the scammer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The scammer actually paid her close to $1,000 on the first day of the engagement, winning her trust.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am sure Members have heard similar sad outcomes for some of our residents and their residents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share how this Bill and the codes of practice will operate to disrupt such scammers, particularly with reference to e-commerce companies, or online service providers through whom such scams are unknowingly perpetrated?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it cannot be left to agencies like the Anti-Scam Command, the Police or even legislation such as this Bill, to serve as the first line of defence for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The general public has to be far more vigilant with respect to its engagements online, especially when it comes to the transfer of funds and engagement with individuals who are not known to them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister let us know what other scenarios beyond criminal activity were discussed or are being deliberated?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the Government previously mentioned that it would seek to address "cancel culture".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could this be one of the areas that is being contemplated as potentially coming within the scope of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: OCHA is targeted at protecting members of the public from scams and offences that can cause financial and other harm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill creates a potentially powerful instrument that can be used to great effect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I shall point out three ways to make this instrument more precise, more powerful and longer in reach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will also focus on the organisational structure as well as the processes that are being contemplated to be put into place to administer and enforce the powers and the responsibilities spelt out in this Bill once it comes into effect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note that the competent authority has a dual role.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this role, it is intended that the “competent authority” be vested with the power to issue Orders for non-compliance of Government Directions to specific entities aimed at proactively dealing with cases where specified criminal offences are suspected to be committed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, it is vested with the responsibility to develop a framework in the form of codes of practice that designated online service providers will have to comply with a view to, amongst others, facilitate information sharing on suspicious online activities and design of features to make online platforms more scam-proof.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To achieve the legislative objective, I foresee the need to foster a relationship of candour, the hon Minister mentioned "partnership" between the online service providers and the competent authority.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The online service providers will need some assurance that if they were to provide inputs in good faith, there will be no serious repercussions against them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Second Minister mentioned that the competent authority will be a unit within the Singapore Police Force (SPF).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder whether this unit within the SPF, will be structurally separated from the investigative arm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will prevent any conflict in the dual roles contemplated for the authority.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One possible example to follow could be the Suspicious Transactions Reports Office (STRO) of the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The STRO has a responsibility in dealing with information-	sharing concerning anti-money laundering activities and others with financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The STRO is sited within the CAD’s intel and admin group, which is separate from CAD’s investigative arm, its financial investigation group.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that it is proposed that the Minister may appoint any public officer from any Ministry, department or an employee from a Statutory Board as an authorised person.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under Clause 5 of the Bill, it is proposed that the competent authority may delegate the exercise of its powers to authorised persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may also issue Directions of a general character to them and they must give effect to the Directions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from the issue of independence that I already raised, it seems to me, given the specialist nature of the duties that will be vested in the competent authority, would it not be better to create a department which can be more focused on developing the expertise and the relations necessary to achieve the legislative objectives of this Bill as opposed to allowing authorised persons to be appointed across the Civil Service?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the Bill, it is the designated officers who will be vested with the power to issue Government Directions in respect of online activity so as to be able to proactively manage suspected crime cases and prevent more people from falling victims to scams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, I am not able to find any direct statutory lever that the competent authority may exercise over the designated officer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is specifically provided though, is that under clause 4(5) of the Bill, a designated officer must act in accordance with his departmental head.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the competent authority has the responsibility to administer the Act once it comes into force and the interplay between the designated officer’s and competent authority’s roles, may I ask why is it felt that it is not necessary to allow the competent authority to issue Directions that the designated officer should heed?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It could be as simple as requiring the designated officer to notify the competent authority at the point when he or she exercises the powers under this Act once it comes into force.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These three points on governance may appear to be quite technical but they go towards sharpening this powerful law against scams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to processes stipulated in the Bill which speaks to the power of this instrument.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first has to do with the status of codes of practice issued by the competent authority.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that it is proposed that the competent authority be vested with, amongst others, the following powers: (a) to stipulate an online service of an online service provider as a designated online service and online service providers as designated providers; and (b) to issue codes of practice that designated providers will have to comply with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Minister mentioned, non-compliance may trigger the issuance of rectification notice and failure to comply with this notice may even be a criminal offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek the hon Minister’s clarification on this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move on to the provisions in the Bill dealing with appeals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that a dual track of appeals is being proposed in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is provided under the respective clauses of the Bill that the decisions of the Minister and the Reviewing Tribunal are final.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question is what is intended by the word “final”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The lawyers in this House would know that Courts do not always interpret “final” as “final”, as if nothing further can be said or challenged.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a good number of cases, the Courts have decided that usage of such words do not oust the jurisdiction of the Courts to judicially review the decisions made on appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, is it contemplated that the Minister and the Reviewing Tribunal will have to provide written grounds of decisions when deciding on appeals so that the Court will be able to properly scrutinise the matter should its jurisdiction to review Government action be invoked?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The “final” here therefore is not incompatible with “still open for challenge”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am glad to note that the offences provided for in this part have extraterritorial reach, having regard to the transnational nature of the scams today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have a query as to why the provision for punishment for the offence created under clause 52, which deals with persons who do not obey a Part 6 Order issued by the competent authority as a result of a failure to comply with a Part 2 Direction, falls below the threshold for making it an extradition offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I understand, clause 6 and clause 28 of the Bill complement each other.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Clause 6 contemplates a designated officer to issue a Part 2 Direction to any person even if he may be located outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The focus here is to proactively deal with situations where certain specified criminal offences are suspected to be committed so as to prevent even more people in Singapore from becoming victims of scams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where any person does not comply with the Part 2 Direction, the competent authority may give a Part 6 Order under clause 28.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This involves, amongst others, the issuance of an Order to the provider of an app distribution service to stop distributing the relevant app to Singapore persons or an Order to a provider of non-compliant online service to suspend or stop the provision of such service to Singapore persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is important to note that it is specifically provided in clause 28 that the recipient of a Part 6 Order may not necessarily be the same as the recipient of the original Part 2 Direction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For a person who fails to comply with a Part 2 Direction, he would have committed an offence under clause 50 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since these provisions are meant to complement each other, may I ask the hon Minister why is there a difference?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would have thought that, having provided these offences to be extraterritorial, it would be important to ensure that the more serious offences in this Bill should be made extradition offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, the fear is that the punishment provisions, insofar as they apply to individuals based outside Singapore, will become toothless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To harmonise the two would allow this instrument a greater, and to my mind, a proper reach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is with these considerations in mind that I have raised some concerns about the Bill in its current form, with attention to its governance structures, the standing of codes of practices issued and its punitive reach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With these issues properly addressed, we will have a stronger legislative instrument suited to fight the rising public menace of online criminal harms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is also supposed to enable swift Government action against online criminal activities, proactively preventing scams and malicious cyber activities to protect potential victims.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Scams are the online criminal activities that loom largest against Singaporeans these days.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I support the Bill, I would like to seek clarification on how the Bill will be able to empower the authorities to deal with scams in ways that existing legislation does not.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This works out to an average of almost $21,000 cheated per case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are staggering amounts of hard-earned savings of Singaporeans lost to scammers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Quite a few victims are my residents who approached me for help to recover their lost savings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Sadly, in most cases, the money had been spirited overseas and could not be recovered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and the Police currently work with Internet service providers to block scam websites.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This means that if a new phishing website was set up to collect usernames and passwords of bank customers, the Government is already empowered to immediately order that website to be blocked, so that no more users in Singapore can access it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What difficulties have the authorities faced in expeditiously blocking actual scam websites, that necessitates the introduction of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note the Minister's explanation in her speech just a moment ago that this Bill will enable authorities to block websites if there is reasonable suspicion that they are being prepared in advance of a scam.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm with the Minister if this means that if someone were to register a domain name that is a variant of, say, "dbs.com", it will get proactively blocked, even if the website does not contain any content yet and even if that domain is registered overseas?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, if a telephone number is reported to have been used to carry out scams, is the Government already empowered to direct telcos to immediately block such numbers?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are there any encumbrances to doing so now that require this Bill?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister previously said that scam calls made over the Internet, such as through messaging apps like WhatsApp, are currently not blocked.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With this Bill, would scam calls made over the Internet now be blocked through an Account Restriction Direction that can be issued to online service providers?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will short message service (SMS) redirection attacks, which redirect text messages containing one-time passwords (OTPs) sent from banks to hackers, be more effectively blocked under this Bill, and if so, how will it be more effectively prevented than under the current regime?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC) and Open Government Products has developed ScamShield, an anti-scam app which automatically blocks scam calls, detects scam messages and allows users to report scam messages and calls.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to note that a version of ScamShield for Android devices has finally been released.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in order for SMSes from known scam numbers to be blocked, a user will need to install the ScamShield app and give the app permissions to read their SMSes and contacts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a multi-step process, which some non-technical users may struggle with.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, even technical users may be reluctant to grant such intrusive access on their phones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This means that more than five million residents in Singapore still do not have ScamShield installed, and presumably more do not have the app setup to block scam messages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These should include those scam phone numbers reported by end users through ScamShield and verified by the NCPC and the Police.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Time is of the essence, since it only takes seconds for an unwitting victim to click on a phishing link and enter their username, password and OTP, and for the scammers to clear out their bank account or Central Provident Fund (CPF) accounts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the ScamShield app, ScamShield bot and website do provide forms for people to report suspected scams, how many people are aware of these reporting channels and actually use them?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government intend to promote its use?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How will they encourage their use and explain it to those who find it challenging, adopting such technology?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The ScamShield bot is able to take in reports of scam messages in non-English languages, but can only reply to users in English.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are there plans to enable it to reply in Chinese, Malay and Tamil, so that more non-English speakers can interact with the bot?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More should be done to leverage the knowledge of the entire population to quickly and comprehensively identify scams, and block scam numbers before more people fall victim to them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can be done through better publicity of these reporting channels, giving updates to users when their reports were used for Police investigations or when the number is blocked, and making it easier for users to report scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I stand in support of the Bill, which seeks to introduce levers to enable the authorities to deal more effectively with online activities that are criminal in nature.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Before I begin, I would like to declare my interest as President of the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will allow the Government to issue Directions to better combat online scams, and this is vital, because just as the e-commerce boom has supercharged the way consumers shop today, it has also led to a sharp increase in online scams in recent years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some of the common complaints by consumers pertaining to e-commerce transactions often involve misleading and false claims, non-delivery of orders and receiving counterfeit products.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To address these complaints, CASE has been advocating for mandatory seller verification by all online marketplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The report said that Nicholas Ong had used separate accounts to perpetuate his scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This shows how important mandatory seller verification is to prevent such scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would therefore like to ask the Minister if the codes of practice that will be issued under this Bill will include mandatory seller verification for e-commerce platforms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If so, what legislative teeth will the codes provide, should platforms refuse to comply?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What will be the threshold, before the competent authority issues a Direction to mandate the implementation of such verification, and will there be a time frame given to the platform to comply with such a Direction?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And if so, what would be the timeframe?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond seller verification, we must put in place a suite of measures to combat e-commerce scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One proposal that I have repeatedly raised is for the Government to require online marketplaces to put in place an escrow account.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a simple but effective mechanism that would serve to protect the consumer's monies until the consumer confirms that the goods bought are delivered in satisfactory condition.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Escrow accounts would give consumers a greater peace of mind when shopping online.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Where there are issues with the goods or in instances of non-delivery of goods, consumers would have the assurance that their monies are protected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would therefore like to ask the Minister if the Bill could require the creation of escrow accounts under the codes of practice or under a Direction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would therefore like to ask the Minister if the e-commerce platforms' key executives will be criminally liable for offences under this Bill, or if they direct their firms not to comply, or to partially comply with the Directions issued.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond legislation, I am happy to share that CASE has been working hard in the past year engaging many industry stakeholders to foster a trusted online marketplace for all consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Including CASE's earlier MOU with Lazada Singapore, we now have two of the leading online marketplaces in Singapore, covering a significant market share of the local e-commerce sales, committed to resolve consumer disputes efficiently and equitably.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I call on all other online marketplaces with local presence to come onboard too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: CASE will also be launching a new CaseTrust accreditation scheme for e-commerce businesses in the second half of this year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The scheme will cover the entire range of e-commerce practices from pre-sale to post-sales and will address common consumer pain points when they shop online.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We hope to provide consumers shopping via accredited e-commerce sites with greater assurance through this accreditation scheme.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This Bill is a timely measure that will allow our authorities to better protect the public in Singapore from various harms in the online space.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the codes of practice and the Directions proposed under this Bill will include measures, such as mandating seller verification and escrow accounts, to better safeguard our consumers when they shop online.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is a significant piece of legislation that will help Singaporeans from online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That night alone, we had three cases of residents facing online scams.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have met many during my house visits and Meet-the-People sessions, many who had fallen victims to the scams or know of someone who had.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With online scams becoming increasingly sophisticated and deploying various methods and technology, I welcome this Bill to combat against online scams and protect our fellow Singapore residents from falling prey.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that the Bill is a necessary step to protect Singaporeans from online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My first clarification is in relation to the appeals process and the oversight of the implementation of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I echo what hon Member Mr Murali Pillai said, "'Final' does not necessarily mean final".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The lawyers would always want to have the final word.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill gives the Minister for Home Affairs broad powers to order Internet intermediaries to remove or block online content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These powers are not subject to judicial oversight, save for an appeal to a Reviewing Tribunal in the case of a Part 2 Direction or an appeal to the Minister or an Appeals Advisory Committee in other appeals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some are concerned about censorship of legitimate content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, firstly, what are the criteria that will be used to determine whether a content is considered to be "online criminal harms"?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My second clarification is in relation to the interim measures pending the conclusion of the appeals stage.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For clauses 17 and 36 of the Bill, there is a requirement that the designated officer or competent authority affirm, cancel or substitute the Direction or Order within a "reasonable time" after receipt of an application for re-consideration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a starting point, I welcome the flexibility given to the relevant authorities to deal with the differing situations that may arise.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because such decisions should be made expeditiously to address the evolving situation and the decision should be made within a reasonable time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, until reconsideration or final decision of an appeal, such decisions and orders remain in force.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My third and final clarification is in relation to keeping up with the forms of online criminal harms using artificial intelligence (AI) or other technological developments.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are faced with new online platforms, media and technology all the time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just earlier this week, Meta announced that it will be launching a new social media app called "Threads" on its Instagram platform rivalling Twitter.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These new platforms and technologies will only increase in number and sophistication as society progresses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, how will MHA be working with MCI or other agencies to ensure this?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In such evolving circumstances, perhaps, the use of AI intervention may be deployed to benefit us, as Member Mr Gerald Giam mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I must say that this must be exercised with caution as the use of AI and other technological tools, comes with its pitfalls and necessary risks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In June 2022, the US Federal Trade Commission issued a report to Congress warning about safeguards when using AI to combat online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The report encourages legislators to create policies that ensure AI tools do not cause additional problems.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some recommendations include avoiding over-reliance due to false positives and false negatives, using more human oversight, improving platform AI interventions and passing laws that change the business models or incentives that allow harmful content to proliferate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore can also be a contributor to the global effort to harmonise the rules of AI regulations and, in particular, by using to detect and deter online criminal harms and also the approach in the case of online criminal harms perpetrated by AI itself.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead of curiosity, we must make our people circumspect when faced with possible scams.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead of arrogance, we must make scammers afraid of the certainty that they will not be able to get away with it.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Online services have become a part of our daily lives and changed how we interact with people, businesses and Government.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The convenience of doing things from the palm of our hands has forever transformed how we live, work and play, bringing new opportunities for people and businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, however, the online space is also increasingly being exploited by criminals and our digital footprint expose us to the risks of scams and malicious cyber activities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has spared no effort in public education and engaging private sector stakeholders, such as banks and telecommunications companies (telcos), to join in the fight against online criminal harms.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As users, we all need to be extra careful and diligent and not let our fingers do the thinking.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A wrong single click may lead to a regret of grave magnitude or even the loss of one's life savings.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As users, we need to unlearn doing everything with speed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With all the instant tools around us, we, in fact, need to relearn how to allow ourselves some time to think and reflect before we act.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not get impatient and frustrated in having to read the repeated warnings about scams and the advice not to release our one-time passwords (OTPs) or to simply click the links in messages without validating.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As spelt out in the First Reading of the Bill and in Minister's speech earlier as well, "complementing public education efforts and the steps being taken to build a discerning citizenry, this Bill enables the Government, in partnership with industry, to act more effectively against online criminal activities, including scams and malicious cyber activities." The Minister has also shared during her Committee of Supply (COS) speech last year that Australia, the UK and the EU are also looking into online safety legislation that provide powers for the authorities to seek take-downs of harmful online content.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I support the approach which will be taken under the proposed Bill, but I do have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will the competent authority qualify "reasonable suspicion"?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How much investigation time will be given to the online services to assist in validating the identity of the suspected perpetrator?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, will the investigation be before or after the directions are issued?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The collaboration of the online service platform providers is imperative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They are the middlemen, so to speak, in the middle of the crime being committed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While the tech industry is committed towards apprehending scams, but compliance may be an issue considering the broad nature of the legislative text.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As most of these online services are global tech companies, they most likely have their own processes and tools and ways of doing things.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How much flexibility will the online service providers have to arrive at the outcomes expected by this Bill?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Cyber criminals often use anonymisation tools and encryption techniques to conceal their identities and activities online.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will MHA handle the challenge of tracing and identifying offenders to take them to task?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, we know, the Internet transcends geographical boundaries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Service providers may also run into issues where data or processes are not stored and run solely in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In some cases, Directions may touch on issues out of jurisdiction and time may be needed to fully comply.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There may be requests that are subject to further legal processes, such as a government-level request under a mutual legal assistance treaty with other countries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Ministry handle the challenge of jurisdictional issues?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is an appeals mechanism within the Bill.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Will the timeline for the adjudication commensurate with the amount of time provided under a relevant Government Direction or will the Government Direction have to be complied with while the appeal is being looked into?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, what technology and capabilities are we investing in to fight this war against online crimes?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In speaking with the industry players, there is appreciation of the consultative approach that the Government has been taking and welcome continued engagement as the Government work on drawing up the codes of practice under this OCHA as this Bill is referred to.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For there to be a win-win-win, this public-private collaboration needs to continue.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can Minister share plans if any, for deepening this collaboration to facilitate the win-win-win?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will empower the Government to issue directions against online activities which may be criminal, act proactively against scams and malicious cyber activities and introduce appeal mechanisms to safeguard the exercise of powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on offences relating to the sale of animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Second Schedule of the Bill sets out offences that the Bill intends to combat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This does not include offences related to the illegal trade of animals and wildlife under the Animals and Birds Act, Wildlife Act and the Endangered Species (Import and Export) Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We know that a significant volume of illegal trade of animals and wildlife is taking place online.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The sellers were unlicensed and the sales illegal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Data published by tech companies highlight the scale of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider including these offences under the Second Schedule?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the nature and effects of the codes of practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 19(4) provides that a requirement of a code of practice has effect despite any duty of confidentiality imposed by any rule of law or a duty imposed by any contract or any rule of professional conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This effectively allows a code of practice to override legislative and contractual rules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, section 21(4) also provides that a code of practice does not have legislative effect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the nature of the code of practice?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A code of practice can be introduced and amended by the competent authority without going through Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would appear inappropriate for such a code to override any duty of confidentiality that is imposed by any rule of law, including any rule introduced by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister give specific examples of rules that the codes may override?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final clarification is on the extraterritorial applications of the provision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 19(2), notices and directives can be given to designated providers even if they are constituted or operating outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Part 11 of the Bill deems non-compliance with Directions and notices to be offences even if committed by persons outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will we ensure implementation of our notices and directives by service providers or individuals located overseas?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the event that a prosecution has to be brought against service providers or individuals located overseas, will steps be taken to secure their attendance in Court?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is one of the most Internet-connected countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Further to this, as the hon Minister said at the Stack 2022 Developer Conference last year, effectively all transactions between citizens and the Government can already be completed digitally end-to-end.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Most of our commercial transactions can also be transacted online, including e-shopping and e-banking.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While this has significantly improved convenience, efficiency and the productivity of Government agencies and commercial entities, it has also increased Singaporeans’ exposure to potential online harms, including scams and other types of criminal activity perpetrated through an online medium.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is, therefore, timely and important to update our laws to deal with new types of criminal offences arising from the online sphere.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Two aspects of the Bill are of particular importance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is important, given the transnational nature of the Internet as regards to users as well as service providers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill provides that liability for various offences have extraterritorial jurisdiction and, likewise, that other measures ordered by the competent authority or designated officer may apply to persons who are not in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the Bill also takes a proactive approach to empower the competent authority to promote or require good practices by designated providers to prevent the commission of various offences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The competent authority may also require designated providers to implement appropriate systems, processes or measures.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This provision will allow the competent authority to pre-empt potential emerging online harms and to take steps to help prevent them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It also grants the competent authority the ability to set out norms for current and new operators and, in this, it is an important preemptive operation of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Arrestable and non-bailable offences are offences in which the Police or the Courts would not normally offer bail, and would consider bail only on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These conditions are imposed for more serious offences and essentially mean that, after being charged, an accused person would be held in remand in prison while waiting for the final verdict.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 50, in particular, criminalises the failure to comply with Orders or Directions made under Part 2 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 6(a) in Part 2 empowers a designated officer to make certain directions if he reasonably suspects that a specified offence has been committed and that online activity is in furtherance of the offence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The specific offences are enumerated at Part 1 of the First Schedule.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My clarification is as regards offences that are listed in Part 1 of the First Schedule that are not arrestable and non-bailable.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, number 32 of Part 1 of the First Schedule reads: “Offences under Part 2 of the Protection from Harassment Act”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These offences include causing fear, alarm or distress and are generally bailable offences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, it may be useful for some clarification from the hon Minister that this may be one of the factors that the Court or the Police could take into account when considering whether to offer bail, which despite being non-bailable, may be offered on a case-by-case basis, for a person charged under clause 50 of the Bill, read with clause 55.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Gone are the days when we could rely on simple indicators like poor English or obvious typos.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By incorporating the Online Criminal Harms Bill into our legislative arsenal, we can enhance our ability to safeguard the public from the perils of the digital realm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, reporting channels must be easily accessible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For this Bill to be successful, people must be willing and know how to come forward to report malicious sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is essential to establish clear and accessible avenues for reporting such sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the designated reporting channels?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Singapore Cyber Emergency Response Team (SingCERT) or IMDA serve as the primary agency to which these sites can be reported?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, what measures are being implemented to ensure that residents find it easy to report these sites?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Increasing awareness and providing user-friendly reporting mechanisms can encourage more individuals to come forward and contribute to the early detection and prevention of online criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to be quick to take action.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the digital era, given the urgency in preventing more victims from falling prey to scams or misinformation, time is of the essence in taking appropriate action against malicious sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would be helpful to understand the time interval between reporting a site and the issuance of any necessary Directions under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister shed light on the timeline or processes involved in evaluating reported sites and initiating the appropriate actions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Swift and timely response is critical in the context of how fast such scams can spread online to minimise the potential harm suffered by unsuspecting individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, virality and reach play a part in determining the impact of the online content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When considering the issuance of Directions, will MHA take into account factors such as the virality and the reach of social media platforms and websites?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important to recognise that platforms with a large following or significant potential for virality can pose a greater risk of rapid and widespread harm, even if their content is equally harmful to that of websites with limited reach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister provide insights into the considerations when assessing the severity and impact of a malicious site?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we should address the means by which individuals or entities might attempt to circumvent the bans on accessing malicious sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While penalties are primarily aimed at non-compliance with Directions, what provisions does the Bill include to address individuals or entities that might modify website addresses or employ other strategies to evade the initial directions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we deter residents from using virtual private network (VPN) or other digital means to access these malicious sites which have been banned?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would be beneficial to understand the measures put in place to mitigate such attempts at circumvention and maintain effective control over the identified malicious sites and apps.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many malicious websites originate overseas, posing challenges in terms of identifying and holding individuals responsible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It raises the important question of how the relevant agency would know whom to direct a Disabling or Restriction Direction to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, why should the creators of such sites who are based overseas comply with such Directions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What penalties do they face and what alternatives do we have, if they refuse?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, in cases where extradition is not feasible due to the absence of an extradition treaty or the foreign enforcement agency's inability to apprehend the overseas culprits, what implications do the penalties outlined in the Bill have for individuals who cannot be brought back to Singapore for prosecution?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the plans and strategies in place to collaborate with foreign counterparts in apprehending these perpetrators and ensuring that they face legal consequences?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What powers does this law have to act on these powerful and subversive entities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With rapid technology advancements which enable growing sophistication of perpetrators, it is imperative that we remain vigilant and adapt our strategies to stay one step ahead.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, we must acknowledge the challenges we face.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One such challenge is the global nature of such crimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As mentioned, many malicious sites and perpetrators are based overseas, making it difficult to bring them to justice promptly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While efforts are being made to collaborate with foreign counterparts, we must accept the limitations and understand that immediate action may not always be possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, the ever-changing nature of scams and online harms necessitates a proactive approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Enforcement, education and awareness remain our key defence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They raised many relevant points which I will do my best to address.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Janet Ang, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Zhulkarnain Rahim had questions in this regard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where there is reasonable suspicion that a specified offence has been committed and that an online activity is, in fact, helping the offence to be carried out, designated officers can issue Directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
