text: In many cases, it would be apparent whether the threshold of “reasonable suspicion” is crossed and action can be taken immediately, for example, child sexual abuse materials that are uploaded onto the Internet.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are quite clear for everyone to see.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In less clear-cut cases, the officers would first carry out investigations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In my opening speech, I had given examples of when the “reasonable suspicion” threshold may not have been crossed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To recap, they include, for example, initial contacting and grooming of victims of scams and blank websites that are not yet activated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are the examples where the "reasonable suspicion" threshold may not have been crossed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, Police action is not unfettered – you have to cross the threshold and the Bill sets the bounds within which the Police can act and beyond which it cannot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Pritam Singh's question, he may have missed my explanation in the opening speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I hope this clarifies the terms that were being used.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip asked how quickly the Government can take action upon detection of online criminal content or activities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where the magnitude of the criminal harm is high, and the impact is spreading fast, the authorities will seek to swiftly nip it in the bud.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police set up the Anti-Scam Command in 2022, and staff from the banks are co-located with Police officers at the Anti-Scam Centre.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This has enabled us to sense-make and act quickly to prevent scams from harming more victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And as I had mentioned in my opening speech, the threshold we have provided in the Bill for taking action against scams, is lower than for other offences, so that we can take action early and swiftly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As far as possible, we do not want to wait until a victim has fallen prey before acting.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Ang and Mr Melvin Yong asked about the responsibilities and expectations that will be placed on online service providers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where we have identified a need for measures to be taken by such companies in order to tackle criminal activities, we would be requiring them in the law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The interventions would be designed with implementation in mind and with emphasis on the outcome more than the how.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This approach recognises that every online platform has its unique features and operating considerations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government will be reasonable in applying the requirements under the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Ms Ang’s comment that there is appreciation of the consultative approach that the Government has been taking in developing this Bill, and her suggestion that such collaboration needs to continue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, in developing the codes of practice, we will engage the online platforms which we intend to designate, and take an outcome-oriented approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also provide reasonable timeframes for platforms to comply with codes and Directives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Ang and Mr Zhulkarnain asked how the Bill may affect privacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, to combat a crime, we can issue Directions to the messaging platform to restrict the accounts which are being used to commit the crime.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We may also require information on the suspected offenders and other platform users involved, in order to fully investigate the case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked that free speech and legitimate content continue to be protected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Article 14 of the Constitution provides such protections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, reasonable boundaries are needed because unfettered and absolute free speech can cause harm to individuals and society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is therefore not uncommon to find laws in some jurisdictions that limit free speech; examples include prohibitions against hate speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope Mr Zhulkarnain will agree this does not create any new criminal offences in respect of speech, nor does it curtail legitimate content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will move on to other queries about the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip, Ms Ang and Mr Louis Ng cited the challenges relating to jurisdictional issues and asked how the Bill will be applicable to websites and online services that are based overseas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We know, however, that some of them may choose not to comply, which is a challenge many countries similarly face.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are further steps that we can then take.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, we can prosecute for non-compliance, where possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, the Bill allows the competent authority to issue Orders to restrict access to the non-compliant online service, to prevent the criminal activity and content from being accessed by persons in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These levers will be used judiciously and only when necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the offence penalties and whether they were decided with extradition in mind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Relatedly, Mr Yong also asked whether we intend to hold key executives of e-commerce platforms criminally liable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We want the executives of online platforms to take online harms seriously and to comply with Directions, but this does not mean they must be personally liable for non-compliance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are more effective measures such as access blocking.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I do not think any executive in his or her right mind would find it easy to explain to their colleagues why because of non-compliance, access has been blocked; and since there is no personal liability, the need for extradition for non-compliance with Directions or Orders is moot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, extradition can be undertaken in respect of the individuals carrying out the underlying specified offences, in accordance with the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would add, however, in the era of user-generated content, a lot of these content creators are very hard to pin down.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we have to ask ourselves what is the priority.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the priority is to prevent harm from continuing to reach our people, you can try and chase down the original perpetrator of the offence or you can try to prevent the harm from happening first.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We want to be able to do both, but we need to be able to nip it in the bud quickly first.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about the factors that will be taken into account, in deciding whether a person should be granted bail when the offence is failure to comply with the Directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A key consideration is the risk profile of the offender.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The nature of the underlying offence, which triggered the issuance of the direction in the first place, will not usually be taken into account, because the essence of the offence is the failure to comply with the Direction issued.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Also, a person liable for non-compliance to a Direction could be an Internet service provider or online service, and thus may not be the perpetrator of the underlying offence to begin with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This shows that the offence of non-compliance and the underlying offence should be assessed separately.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip asked how the Bill would relate to existing legislation such as FICA and POFMA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: POFMA and FICA were designed specifically to handle online falsehoods and foreign interference respectively, and will continue to be used for such threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We recognise, however, that some cases are complex and levers under multiple legislation could apply.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will consider the unique aspects of each case and use the appropriate levers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Here, it may be useful for me to address a point that Mr Gerald Giam made.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I believe he asked specifically that we already have some levers under the Broadcasting Act, when the Online Safety Bill was passed and now we are trying to pass the Online Criminal Harms Bill – what is it that the new Bill will do that we were not able to do in the previous legislation?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Perhaps it is useful to then compare and contrast more broadly what this set of legislation or legislative tools are designed to achieve that we were not able to do previously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First is in terms of the scope of content that is covered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amended Broadcasting Act covers egregious content as defined in the Act, with the key focus on online safety, including content advocating or instructing on suicide, or self-harm, content posing public health risk in Singapore and content likely to cause racial and religious disharmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, those were the kinds of things that we covered last year, when we debated the Online Safety Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the scope of coverage is not identical.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They overlap to some extent but are also not identical.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amended Broadcasting Act applies to online communication services, but as a start, only social media services are subject to the provisions under the amended Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Online Criminal Harms Bill will cover all mediums of online communications through which criminal activities could be conducted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Thirdly, the levers to deal with scams and malicious cyber activities are quite different.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Broadcasting Act's code of practice for online safety will require social media services to respond to user reports on scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is the part that is quite key.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It has not necessarily taken place, but it looks to be, from past cases, that this is preparation in service of that offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There will also be requirements for the designated online services to put in place proactive measures to detect and minimise scams and malicious cyber activities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, those are the three areas where the two differ; and the two actually complement each other.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali asked about the structure and delineation of roles between the competent authority, authorised officer and designated officer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He suggested that given the role of the competent authority, it should operate separately from the investigation arm of a law enforcement agency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In building up the competent authority’s office, the appointment of authorised officers by the Minister will take into account the expertise and relationships required to effectively administer the Bill, as Mr Murali has pointed out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Designated officers would be those who are charged with detecting, enforcing, or investigating the specified offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They would be best placed to determine whether and what kind of Directions should be issued, and will do so independently of the competent authority.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Administratively, we intend for there to be a single point of contact to issue the Directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This function will reside with the competent authority.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The competent authority will therefore have an overall picture of all the Directions being issued.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Singh asked for the details of the codes of practice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yong asked whether the codes of practice could include requirements for e-commerce platforms, such as seller verification and escrow accounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Requirements for designated e-commerce platforms will take reference from the E-commerce Marketplace Transaction Safety Ratings (TSR).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The TSR is a publicly available report that rates major e-commerce platforms based on the anti-scam measures they have in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The higher the rating, the more anti-scam features a platform has.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I encourage members of the public to refer to the TSR when transacting online and exercise caution when transacting on platforms with lower ratings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When engaging your residents on how to protect themselves from scams, Members can also encourage your residents to refer to the TSR when transacting online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali and Mr Ng had queries on the technical provisions in the codes of practice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Codes of practice issued under clause 21(4) of the Bill do not have legislative effect.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means that they do not constitute law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such provisions are common for codes of practice under Singapore legislation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In our case, given the fast-evolving nature of the online space, we anticipate that the competent authority may need to adjust provisions in the codes of practice every now and then, to keep pace with emerging threats and industry developments, including tailoring the codes to different types of online services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is similar to how licensing conditions in regulated sectors are today determined and varied as necessary by the licensing authority.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also be able to take action if any provision of the codes are not complied with, which Mr Yong was also concerned about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In such instances, the competent authority is empowered to issue a rectification notice to a non-compliant entity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will be an offence under this Bill if the designated online service does not comply with the notice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ng asked about the provision that the requirements of a code of practice have effect, despite duties imposed by any rule of law, contract, or rule of professional conduct.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This clause is similar to provisions under POFMA and the amended Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As an example, one rule of law is the obligation of confidentiality under contract or common law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, with the said provision in this Bill, an online service cannot reject a requirement to provide information on the basis that it is under an obligation of confidentiality.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To reassure Mr Ng, the competent authority cannot issue any code as it pleases.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Any code being considered must fulfil the purpose set out in the Third Schedule.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Any amendments to the Third Schedule must be presented to Parliament.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Ang and Mr Zhulkarnain asked whether Directions and Orders will need to be complied with while the reconsideration or the appeal is ongoing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To reassure Members, we have provided within the Bill that the Reviewing Tribunal must complete its work expeditiously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On Mr Murali's question about the finality of appeals made to the Minister or to the Reviewing Tribunal, there is no ouster clause within this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Decisions made by the Minister and the Reviewing Tribunal will be documented and can be subject to judicial review.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked that the Bill be periodically reviewed to keep up-to-date with evolving online criminal harms and the state of technology.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bill has been drafted with this in mind, allowing us to add further offences via amendments to the First and Second Schedules, where necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA will work closely with other agencies to monitor developments in the technology space and respond nimbly to threats that can be posed by emerging technology, such as generative AI.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Singh asked what other harms the Online Criminal Harms Act might cover in future.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ng asked about the inclusion of offences relating to the sale of animals, birds and wildlife.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will consider Mr Ng's suggestion in future reviews.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to other harms, they must be criminal in nature and have an online nexus.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Ang had queries about the information request provisions for investigating underlying offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we seek to investigate cases expeditiously, we will set reasonable timelines for online services to comply with such requests.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Next, I will deal with the questions and suggestions which relate to our broader efforts against online criminal harms and scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Strictly, these fall outside the scope of today's Bill and some of them have been discussed in this House before.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With respect to the points made by Mr Singh regarding other legislation, these have already been debated in great detail on previous occasions, and they have no bearing on today's Bill in particular.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first is that I believe Mr Singh mentioned POFMA and that with POFMA, the Government decides what is truth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that is not quite a correct characterisation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Singh knows very well that POFMA deals with false statements of fact.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These false statements of fact can be proven.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There has to be a basis for making those allegations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Opinions – people are free to continue to make.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But if you say something that is factually incorrect and it is carried online, it can go very far and it has public interest, and that is where POFMA could be considered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Other than that, opinions – anyone is free to continue to offer theirs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second point is that in the vast majority of the cases where POFMA directions have been issued, the receivers have complied in full and the content they had put up originally remain fully accessible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most of the POFMA directions are like that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Anyone can still read what was originally made available.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To the third point, Mr Pritam Singh specifically mentioned Asia Sentinel.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I do not wish to go into that in great detail because it has no bearing on the Bill we are debating.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would invite him, if he is very interested, to file a Parliamentary Question and we can address his concerns.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Ang asked what technology and capabilities the Government is investing in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the speed and scale at which online criminal harms can be perpetrated, manual processes will not be effective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In implementing AI, we will keep in mind the potential downsides as shared by Mr Zhulkarnain.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In line with Mr Yip's suggestions, we will continue to work with agencies such as the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) to make reporting channels for the public more easily accessible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On Ms Ang's and Mr Yip's queries about overseas perpetrators, cooperation across borders is needed to take them to task.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will certainly continue to strengthen our international partnerships.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip asked how we would deal with attempts by members of the public to circumvent the Directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We cannot protect people who deliberately avoid the protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip, and I believe, Mr Giam, also called for greater efforts to educate the public and to sensitise them to the threat of online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police have worked with several stakeholders to educate the public and raise awareness on scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police have also set up the Scam Public Education Office to drive anti-scam outreach, which will involve working closely with community partners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Scam Public Education Office will collaborate with the National Crime Prevention Council to create and curate anti-scam educational content for the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will partner the private sector and community agencies to tailor anti-scam material for different population groups such as youths and seniors, migrant workers, banking services users and digital platform users.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: SPF also works closely with the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) and the IMDA to develop joint cybersafe materials and participate in public events to share the materials with members of the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some examples include the Digital for Life Festival organised by IMDA and the sharing on the safe use of the internet by IMDA's Digital Ambassadors with seniors in particular.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I know this is a group that Mr Yip is particularly concerned about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have on my notes here points that were made by Mr Giam with respect to calls.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think he said that shutting down websites is one thing – what about calls?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Actually, the topic of whether calls should be blocked has been covered separately.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think in previous updates on anti-scam measures, we had talked about the fact that IMDA implements call blocking on a very wide scale.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is either every single day, every single week or every single month; any way, it is 55 million – a big number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I must caution that our developers are mindful that we do not go beyond what people expect of privacy protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is them exercising a degree of self-restraint.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In discussing such issues with my colleagues from other jurisdictions – I shall not mention where – where the population is much more accustomed to a far higher degree of surveillance, yes indeed, some of these measures can go a lot further.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am mindful, and I think Members have continued to remind us that there is only so much you can do and there are certain thresholds we should not cross.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is another important step towards creating a safer online space for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It complements existing efforts to act more effectively against online criminal activities, through partnerships with our people, the Government and industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I still have a few outstanding questions on which I need a bit more clarification.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: If someone were to register a domain name that is a variant of a bank's website and there is reasonable suspicion that there might be plans to impersonate the bank, can this website be proactively blocked under clause 6(1)(b) even if that website does not contain any content yet?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I just want some clarification on that point.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Minister also did not answer my questions about SMS redirection – whether or not SMS redirection attempts will be or can be blocked under this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These websites can be spawned in the millions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are so many permutations that the scammers can think of.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As much as the Police would like to be able to shut them down, I must caution that we do not expect that they will all be eliminated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, I think in terms of WhatsApp, WhatsApp has end-to-end encryption.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, you and I actually can report a user who makes contact with us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Any message that you receive from an unwelcome party, you can make a request to the service provider, and the service providers have their own policies as to whether it is blocked or not.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to the question of whether the levers within this Bill can apply to WhatsApp – yes, if we believe that there is an underlying offence that is being carried out and there is some indication as to how it is being perpetuated through this particular communication service.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On SMS redirection – I am afraid I am not very clear about the nature of the Member's question.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Perhaps I could trouble him to explain it to me a little bit more.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It is the situation where a bank sends out an SMS One-time Password (OTP) meant for the customer but it gets redirected to a scammer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, the scammer receives the OTP and is then able to enter it to complete the transfer of funds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This is how some Singaporeans have fallen victim to it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It happened during the OCBC scandal, I think, at the end of 2021.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, I just want to find out whether or not this Bill will cover and be able to prevent such actions from being taken.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What you have described as SMS redirection, we have dealt with it earlier at two levels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What you described as SMS interception very often refers to victims unknowingly giving up their credentials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If it is a technical issue, the gap has been plugged.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If it is a matter of individuals being tricked or being deceived into giving up their credentials, then that is quite another matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I refer to the points I made about related legislation, FICA and POFMA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I brought them up because of the statement released by MHA when the Bill came up for First Reading, the comparison that was made about this being a suite of legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I take the Minister's point about pursuing a query I made in my speech through a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My question relates to the point I made about the scam that affected my resident earlier, specifically with regard to e-commerce websites that are part of this whole chain of scam activities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Then, from WhatsApp, you get a payment through PayNow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The question I have is with e-commerce platforms like Qoo10, when there is an encouragement for an innocent person to be part of an enterprise where you click on a feature of that website which raises the profile of some products on sale, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: How do the codes of practice, for example – what sort of influence will they have on these online service providers and these e-commerce companies to address that sort of problem which actually tends to direct more traffic to their website anyway?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am just trying to understand how the codes of practices will compel a certain behaviour to address the scams we have to deal with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, you must be able to catch the perpetrators.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One of the difficulties of many of these platforms is that your identity can be shielded.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the platform does not really know who you are.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, one of the requirements of the codes of practice – I say this with the caveat, and I hope Members understand this – the codes of practice have yet to be published, even in draft form.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We may impose certain requirements through the code on service providers in determining a user authentication process.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is one area of intervention that could be fruitful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I mentioned this in relation to the TSR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You could think of the TSR as something that we have put out on a voluntary basis.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But if you introduce a code of practice, then you are essentially saying to service providers that you now need to introduce these measures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yong talked about an escrow account, but that is not the only way in which you can assure the buyer using any particular platform, any e-commerce platform, that he has not been deceived.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Only upon his confirmation of the receipt of the goods is the money released to the purported seller.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are two broad areas of interventions that could be helpful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I would encourage Members to watch out for when the draft codes are actually published.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At that time, you are certainly welcome to give your views.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: There being no further clarifications, I will put the question.      .
